walkthroughs.body_html:
Activity is how fast a source decays, measured in becquerel (Bq). 1 Bq = 1 decay per second.

Activity halves every half-life, just like the number of nuclei.

Dose in sieverts (Sv) tells you the biological harm. High doses kill cells; low doses can mutate DNA and raise cancer risk.

Smoke detectors: a tiny alpha source ionises air. Smoke blocks the ions, alarm triggers.

Medical tracers: short half-life gamma emitters track blood flow or organs.

Cancer treatment: focused gamma rays kill tumour cells (radiotherapy).

Sterilisation: gamma rays kill bacteria on surgical tools and food without heating them.

Fission: a big nucleus (like U-235) absorbs a neutron and splits. Releases energy + more neutrons → chain reaction. Used in nuclear power stations.

Fusion: two small nuclei (like hydrogen isotopes) join to make a bigger one. Powers the Sun. Needs huge temperature and pressure.

options: 50 Bq
100 Bq
200 Bq
400 Bq

mcqs.q: Which is the BEST radiation for a medical tracer injected into the body?
options: Long half-life alpha
Long half-life beta
Short half-life gamma
Short half-life alpha

mcqs.q: Which type of nuclear radiation is most ionising?
options: Gamma is most ionising because it can travel furthest and pass through almost anything.
Alpha radiation — large, doubly charged particles cause the most ionisation per unit distance.
Beta radiation is most ionising because it consists of fast electrons.
Fusion is harder because you need to break atoms apart first.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between nuclear fission and fusion?
options: Fission combines small atoms into bigger ones, and fusion splits them.
Fission and fusion are the same process, just at different scales.
Fission splits a heavy nucleus into smaller ones; fusion joins light nuclei into a heavier one.
Beta radiation is most ionising because it consists of fast electrons.

mcqs.q: Why is nuclear fusion much harder to achieve on Earth than fission?
options: Fusion is harder because the materials are rarer than uranium.
Beta radiation is most ionising because it consists of fast electrons.
Fusion requires extremely high temperatures and pressures to overcome the electrostatic repulsion between positive nuclei.
Fusion is harder because you need to break atoms apart first.
